claims.claim: The subject is the House discharge petition
claims.sourceSpan: The House discharge rule (Rule XV, clause 2) provides a means for Members to bring to the floor for consideration a public bill or resolution that has been referred to committee but not reported.

claims.claim: A discharge petition brings a measure to the floor without cooperation from the committee, the majority-party leadership or the Rules Committee
claims.sourceSpan: generally the only procedure by which Members can secure consideration of a measure without cooperation from the committee(s) of referral, the majority-party leadership, or the Committee on Rules

claims.claim: The threshold is 218 signatures
claims.sourceSpan: was construed to mean 218 Members (Speaker Byrns, Apr. 15, 1936, p. 5509)

claims.claim: Its data cover 1931 through 2002
563 petitions filed, 47 reached the signature threshold, 26 discharge votes, 19 measures passed the House, two became law and two others changed House Rules
claims.sourceSpan: 563 discharge petitions have been filed, of which 47 obtained the required signatures. The House voted for discharge 26 times, and passed 19 of the measures involved, but only two became law (and two others changed House Rules).

claims.claim: The indirect route: 10 completed-petition measures considered under other procedures with eight becoming law; 32 pending-petition measures taken up, all but three passing the House and 17 receiving final approval
claims.sourceSpan: The House considered 10 of the measures on which petitions were completed, under other procedures, and eight of these became law. It also took up, under other procedures, 32 measures on which petitions were still pending. Of these, all but three passed the House, and 17 received final approval.

claims.claim: CRS overall figure: about 16% of discharge attempts ended in completion or floor action by some means
claims.sourceSpan: either the petition was completed, or the measure received floor action by some means, in about 16% of discharge attempts

claims.claim: R45920 records a pronounced recent increase in petitions filed and in those reaching 218
claims.sourceSpan: Few measures subjected to the discharge process have reached the House floor in recent decades, but there has been a pronounced increase in recent Congresses both in the number of discharge petitions filed and the number that collected 218 signatures.

claims.claim: Two efforts reached the threshold in the 118th Congress and four in the first session of the 119th
claims.sourceSpan: Two discharge efforts in the 118 th Congress (2023-2024) reached the threshold, and four did so in the first session of the 119 th Congress (2025).

claims.claim: CRS: use of discharge can challenge the agenda-setting responsibilities of the Speaker and majority leadership, and the Rules Committee might respond with its own rule
claims.sourceSpan: The use of the discharge procedure can challenge the agenda-setting responsibilities of the Speaker and the majority leadership. Consequently, if a discharge petition approaches or receives the required 218 signatures, the Committee on Rules might respond by reporting its own rule for considering the measure, or an alternative to it, perhaps based on negotiations with supporters of the discharge effort.

claims.claim: The seven-legislative-day calendar wait is the window in which the Rules Committee would normally call up its own rule
claims.sourceSpan: The Rules Committee would normally call up its own rule at some point during the period of seven legislative days a discharge motion must remain on the Calendar

claims.claim: If the alternative rule is adopted the measure is considered on the Rules Committee terms, not the discharged rule terms
claims.sourceSpan: it can consider the measure the rule makes in order, but under the terms proposed by the Committee on Rules, not those prescribed by the rule subject to the discharge process

claims.claim: A discharge on an unreported measure becomes moot if the committee reports it first
claims.sourceSpan: A discharge process on an unreported measure becomes moot, however, if the committee to which a discharge effort is directed reports the measure before the motion is offered. Since it no longer has possession of the measure, the committee cannot be discharged from considering it.

claims.claim: A discharge aimed at a special rule survives the committee reporting the underlying measure
claims.sourceSpan: if a committee reports a measure after a special rule for considering it is introduced, a discharge attempt on the rule providing for that measure's consideration remains valid

claims.claim: CRS gives that as a reason proponents aim at a special rule they introduce themselves

claims.claim: After discharge the measure may be considered in Committee of the Whole under the five-minute rule or in the House under the one-hour rule
claims.sourceSpan: Once a committee is discharged, the measure may be considered in Committee of the Whole under the five-minute rule, or in the House under the one-hour rule, depending on the nature of the measure itself.

claims.claim: For a money measure the next motion in order is to resolve into Committee of the Whole
claims.sourceSpan: If the measure is a "money measure" (including authorization, appropriation, and revenue measures), the next motion in order is that the House resolve into Committee of the Whole to consider it.

claims.claim: REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep): "218 signatures - a majority of the House's 435 members." The 435 figure appears in no stored source (grepped across all of data/ref-text/). The page now gives the rule's own phrase, "a majority of the total membership of the House," and the Manual annotation construing it as 218 Members with the date and Congressional Record page.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep, worst finding on this page): the paragraph attributing a behavioural claim about leadership scheduling to nobody - originally "what analysts call the threat effect", already softened before this audit to "Leadership can see a petition approaching 218 signatures, and a vote on the measure, or on an alternative, is sometimes scheduled before the petition reaches that threshold." Neither version had a source. It is replaced with the CRS 97-856 indirect-success counts, which measure the same phenomenon with published figures: 10 completed-petition measures and 32 pending-petition measures taken up under other procedures, and the ~16% overall figure.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "Most bills that die in the House die because a committee chair or the majority leadership never schedules them, and there is usually nothing rank-and-file members can do about it," and "It is rarely completed, but its existence shapes what leadership chooses to bring up on its own." Both unsourced. The lede is now the CRS characterisation of what discharge is for and why it is hard.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "That number is the whole point: it means a discharge petition can only succeed when an actual majority of the House wants the measure considered, which is precisely the situation in which the majority-party leadership's refusal to schedule a bill is overriding what the chamber as a whole would do," and the parallel "Setting the bar at a full majority is what ties the procedure to genuine chamber-wide support rather than a determined minority." Both are the article evaluating the rule rather than reporting it.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): the whole "The shift matters because it changes the political dynamics" paragraph - "a member can quietly decline to sign without any public consequence", "Publicity turns the petition from a private headcount into an open pressure campaign." Motive and effect claims with no source. Replaced with the Manual's own record of how the 1993 change came about (itself through a successful discharge petition against the Rules Committee), the later amendments, and the publication duties the rule actually imposes on the Clerk.
CORRECTED: the article said "just 2 ultimately became law" and stopped there. CRS 97-856 says "only two became law (and two others changed House Rules)." The parenthetical is now included.

CORRECTED: "an additional 7 legislative days must elapse before the motion becomes eligible to be called up" omitted two conditions in the same sentence of the rule - the exception "during the last six days of a session of Congress", and the requirement that a signatory announce an intention to offer the motion, after which the Speaker designates a time within two legislative days. Both are now stated.

CORRECTED and reconciled: the article dated the 218 threshold to 1935 with no source. Both dates are real and they describe different things. CRS 97-856 records that the 1935 amendment raised the requirement from 145 (one-third) to 218 (one-half); the House Manual records that the rule's own phrase, "a majority of the total membership of the House," was construed to mean 218 Members by Speaker Byrns on April 15, 1936. The page now states the rule change, the ruling, and which is which.

ADDED from R45920 and the rule text: the Rules Committee discharge route, which CRS says is now the more common form, along with the procedural reason (proponents draft the special rule themselves and set the terms), the no-motion-to-proceed consequence, and the rule's two limits (one measure only, no nongermane amendment; only one motion per measure). The pre-refresh article did not mention that a discharge petition can be aimed at the Rules Committee at all.

ADDED from the rule text: adoption of a discharge motion does not by itself bring the measure up. Clause 2(d)(2)'s privileged, non-debatable motion to proceed - available only to a signatory - and the consequence of its rejection were absent from the pre-refresh page.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NON-BLOCKING, adjudicated against hman-119-rule-xv.txt and confirmed): clause 2(e) was omitted entirely. Once the House has acted on a discharge motion, no motion to discharge on the same measure - or on any measure substantially the same in substance or subject matter - is in order for the rest of the session, and a motion rendered out of order is stricken from the discharge calendar. A reader could not tell from the pre-fix draft that discharge is effectively one attempt per subject per session.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NON-BLOCKING): the draft gave only the rejected-motion-to-proceed outcome. Clause 2(d)(2) also states what happens on adoption - immediate consideration under the general rules of the House, and unfinished-business status if not disposed of that day - which is now on the page alongside the special-rule outcome CRS supplies.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NOTE): clause 2(c)(1) also bars intervening motions except one motion to adjourn while a discharge motion is being considered, and orders competing privileged discharge motions by their entry on the Journal. Both added.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NOTE): the withdrawal quote dropped the mechanism. The rule says a signature may be withdrawn "by a Member in writing at any time before a motion is entered on the Journal"; the page and this ledger row now carry the full span.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NON-BLOCKING): the meta description, og:description and JSON-LD description all said a discharge petition forces a bill to the floor "over the objection of leadership." The source says "without cooperation from the committee(s) of referral, the majority-party leadership, or the Committee on Rules" - absence of cooperation, not active objection. All three now track the source, and the articles-index card summary was changed to match.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NON-BLOCKING): the ledger carried a row for "Only one motion may be presented for a bill or resolution" that no draft sentence expressed. Rather than prune the row, the rule was added to the prose, where it belongs next to the clause 2(e) repeat bar.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NOTE): the closing section said discharge is "one of several routes to the floor that do not require the Rules Committee to act" - a count none of this page's sources make. It now names the specific clauses of the same Rule XV the page is already sourced to: suspension (cl. 1), the Private Calendar (cl. 5), Calendar Wednesday (cl. 6) and the Consensus Calendar (cl. 7), each with a receipt.

ROUND 2, ACCEPTED AS IS (hostile Sonnet verifier, NOTE): three quoted spans begin mid-sentence with the source's sentence-initial capital lowercased ("For this reason", "Under the previous form", "In modern practice"). Standard splice convention, no word changed and no meaning altered; the receipts on this ledger carry the source capitalisation, and qa-receipts matching is case-insensitive.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, BLOCKING, adjudicated against record-crs-r45920-discharge-procedure.txt and CONFIRMED): the page said the 1931-2002 CRS 97-856 numbers were "the only complete count that has been published" and that CRS "has not published an updated series in the reports stored here." Both statements were false against a source already on this ledger. R45920 (updated 2026-02-12) carries a whole section, Recent Use of the Discharge Process, reporting a pronounced recent increase - two efforts reaching 218 in the 118th Congress and four in the first session of the 119th, with named rules, named underlying measures and public-law numbers. Omitting it left the page telling readers discharge effectively never works while the current source says the opposite about recent Congresses. The section is rewritten around both datasets, each labelled with its vintage.

ROUND 3 ADDITION (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): the page explained the special-rule route without the fact that makes it worth using. A discharge on an unreported MEASURE becomes moot if the committee reports the measure first; a discharge on a SPECIAL RULE for that measure "remains valid" in the same circumstance. Both now quoted.

ROUND 3 ADDITION (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): what happens after a successful motion to proceed was given only from the rule text. R45920 supplies the practical answer - Committee of the Whole under the five-minute rule or the House under the one-hour rule depending on the measure, with money measures going to Committee of the Whole - and the germaneness limit that applies to a measure taken up in introduced form.

ROUND 3 ADDITION (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): the unsourced "threat effect" paragraph removed in round 1 had a sourced counterpart in R45920 that the draft never used. CRS states that discharge "can challenge the agenda-setting responsibilities of the Speaker and the majority leadership" and that the Rules Committee "might respond by reporting its own rule", normally during the seven-legislative-day calendar period, with the measure then considered on the committee terms. This is the same phenomenon the removed paragraph gestured at, now on the record and attributed.

SOURCING NOTE: the mechanics are now anchored to CRS R45920 (updated February 12, 2026) rather than to CRS 97-856 (April 17, 2003), which is used only for the historical counts it actually reports. R45920 publishes no updated statistical series, so the 1931-2002 figures are labelled with their end date and their vintage on the page rather than presented as current practice. The dead congress.gov/crs-product/R45920 link was replaced with the everycrsreport mirror that was actually fetched and read.
REMOVED from Key Sources: the House Practice Chapter 19 link (govinfo GPO-HPRACTICE-108). Nothing on the page was drawn from it in this rewrite, and the Key Sources box lists sources actually used.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING, adjudicated against record-crs-r45920-discharge-procedure.txt and CONFIRMED): the recent-use passage said "all six" targeted a special rule but narrated only four outcomes, dropping H.Res. 164 and H.Res. 581.
